title: Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorems

body: Kurt Gödel's 1931 paper, "Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme I," shows that a consistent formal system strong enough for elementary arithmetic is incomplete. There are statements in its language that the system does not prove and does not refute, if the system is consistent. A related result is that such a system cannot prove its own consistency, again if it is consistent. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry on Gödel's incompleteness theorems is a guide to the scope and the limits of these results. They are theorems about formal systems that can represent enough arithmetic. They are not a finding that mathematics is arbitrary, and they do not say that every interesting question is undecidable. A system can be extended. The extended system has its own undecidable sentences. That is the shape of the result.
